disease_label_per_paper: Varicella zoster virus encephalitis in a kidney transplant recipient with recent shingles
presentation_summary: 67-year-old man with kidney transplant, chronic renal dysfunction, and prior CMV retinitis with vision loss had multiple healthcare encounters over three weeks.
He developed a painful vesicular rash along the right second sacral dermatome and was prescribed oral valacyclovir for shingles, later renal-dose adjusted because of chronic kidney disease.
He developed vivid visual hallucinations, word-finding difficulty, generalized weakness, and difficulty ambulating.
At the fourth emergency department visit he was afebrile-to-low-grade at 99.4 F, hypertensive at 196/91 mmHg, and had crusted S2 dermatomal lesions on the posterior right leg.
Neurologic examination showed generalized weakness and gait difficulty without focal neurologic deficits.
Labs were otherwise unremarkable except BUN 23.1 mg/dL, creatinine 3.03 mg/dL, and estimated GFR 22 mL/min.
Brain CT showed only chronic mild-to-moderate degenerative changes; CSF showed elevated protein with lymphocyte predominance, and CSF PCR detected VZV on hospital day 1.

Brain MRI showed chronic microvascular ischemia and abnormal distal left vertebral artery appearance; teams diagnosed VZV encephalitis in the context of recent shingles, CSF findings, and presentation.
He received IV acyclovir and completed a two-week course with improvement in hallucinations and presenting symptoms before discharge.

quality_warnings: The paper reports elevated CSF protein with lymphocyte predominance but does not give exact CSF numeric values; only parent CSF inflammation and approximate lymphocyte fraction are encoded.
MRI vascular abnormality was nonspecific/chronic and is encoded as low vasculopathic imaging activity.
VZV PCR is retained as rankable structured microbiologic evidence because pathogen identity is central to this disease leaf and cannot reliably emerge from routine CSF or imaging alone.
